I hit the tool limit before I could read anything from netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, the Catholic and Orthodox sites, the Lutheran sites, or any prosperity or hyper-grace teaching, so those sections are missing below. I only labelled a commentator's tradition where the page itself does.

## 1. The traditional reading, verse by verse

**vv. 29–30 (houses in walled cities)**
- The seller of a city house can buy it back for one year. After that it belongs to the buyer for good, and the Jubilee doesn't return it. Guzik quotes Rooker's reason: city houses weren't part of the family's inherited land and weren't critical to its survival. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-25/
- Matthew Henry says city houses came from people's own work, while country land was God's direct gift. That's why city houses get only a year's grace. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/leviticus/25.htm
- A commentary on Bible Hub (I couldn't tell which; it comes just before Benson's) says buildings are man's work, not God's allotment, so the Jubilee doesn't cover them. The year protects an owner who is attached to his home. During the Second Temple period the seller wasn't allowed to buy it back with borrowed money. Benson adds that the rule encouraged strangers and converts to settle. Keil and Delitzsch explain the Hebrew phrase "days" as meaning a fixed period of one year. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/25-29.htm
- Gill says the seller or a near relative could buy it back on any day within the year, which Maimonides counted as a solar year of 365 days. A field, by contrast, couldn't be bought back for two years. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/25-29.html
- The Biblical Illustrator calls the year a "year of deliberation." It protects against pressure, careless sales and hardship. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/25-31.html
- Bible Hub's study notes say the one-year limit stops the seller acting rashly without leaving the buyer uncertain forever. City houses weren't part of Israel's covenant inheritance. https://biblehub.com/leviticus/25-30.htm

**v. 31 (unwalled villages)**
- Village houses count as farmland. They can be bought back at any time and go back to the owner at the Jubilee. https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_25_commentary
- Clarke and Benson agree. Benson says village houses were part of the farmland they served. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/25-29.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/25-29.htm
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB) says village houses were tied to farming, while walled-town houses belonged to traders or foreigners. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/25-29.htm

**vv. 32–34 (Levites' houses and pastureland)**
- Matthew Henry: Levites can buy back their houses at any time, and the houses return at the Jubilee. The Levites had no other property, and God wanted to show they were in his special care. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lev/Lev_025.cfm
- The Pulpit Commentary: these houses were the tribe of Levi's share of the national property, so they work like land does for the other tribes. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/leviticus-25.html
- Keil and Delitzsch: when a non-Levite bought a Levite's house, he was really buying back land his own tribe had given up for the Levites. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/25-48.html
- Coffman: there may be an ambiguity in v. 33. A marginal reading adds "not," so the verse would be about a Levite's house that wasn't bought back. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/25-29.html

**vv. 35–38 (the poor brother, and interest)**
- Ellicott: "his hand wavered" means he can no longer support himself, and "relieve him" literally means "lay hold of him." These verses cover the brother who is waiting for his land to come back at the Jubilee. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/25-35.htm
- Keil and Delitzsch: take him by the arm and help him out of his trouble. The Geneva Bible notes read the shaking hand as a hand held out for help. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/25-35.htm
- Gill: he might be poor through illness, family trouble or business losses, not laziness. He should be lent money without interest to get him working again. "Fear thy God" because God sees hidden demands for payment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/25-35.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/25-36.html
- Pulpit: the words "or increase" stop people getting round the law by demanding back more food or goods than they lent. The law was broken in Nehemiah's time (Neh. 5:7–8). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/25-35.htm
- Guzik: the passage forbids profiting from a brother's misfortune. He links it to Luke 6:34 and cites Ezekiel listing usury among serious crimes. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-25/
- Matthew Henry on v. 38: God uses the same reason that opens the Ten Commandments. People who have received mercy should show mercy. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lev/Lev_025.cfm

**vv. 39–43 (an Israelite who sells himself)**
- Ellicott: only poverty would make an Israelite sell his freedom. He mustn't be given the menial work of foreign slaves; Second Temple teachers listed jobs like helping a master at the bath or tying his sandals. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/25-39.htm
- Gill: he might be sold by himself or, for theft, by the court (Ex. 22:3). He should do farm or craft work and be treated more like a brother. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/25-39.htm
- Keil and Delitzsch: he is to be a day-labourer, not a slave (compare Ex. 1:14). At the Jubilee he and his children go back to the family land. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/25-39.htm
- Matthew Henry on v. 42: the master doesn't own him the way someone owns a war captive. "God does not make his servants slaves, and therefore their brethren must not." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lev/Lev_025.cfm
- Constable: masters were to treat these men as brothers. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/25-39.html

**vv. 44–46 (slaves from other nations)**
- Ellicott: slaves could be bought only from neighbouring peoples (Ammonites, Moabites, Edomites, Syrians), not from the seven nations of Canaan (Deut. 20:16–18). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/25-44.html
- Keil and Delitzsch: foreign slaves could be passed on to one's children, but Israelites could not be made to do slave labour. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/25-44.htm
- Coffman: he separates "the nations around you" (v. 44) from foreigners living in the land (v. 45). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/25-44.html

**vv. 47–53 (redemption from a foreign owner)**
- Calvin: "strangers" means only foreigners living in Canaan. The aim was that none of God's adopted people would be cut off from their people and from true worship. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/25-47.html
- Matthew Henry: an Israelite sold to a foreigner was better protected than one sold to an Israelite, because his relatives could buy him back. Jewish tradition says that if they didn't, the community should pay (Neh. 5:8). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lev/Lev_025.cfm
- Gill on v. 49: the Targums take "uncle" as the father's brother. The redeemer had to be a near relative, and the Hebrew word go'el means both. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/25-49.html
- JFB on vv. 50–52: the price was the current wage multiplied by the years left until the Jubilee. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/25-44.htm
- Pulpit on v. 53: he must be treated kindly, and his countrymen must watch that he isn't treated too harshly. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/25-48.html

**vv. 54–55 (release at the Jubilee)**
- Calvin: if no relative helps, he goes free at the Jubilee, along with all Abraham's children. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/25-47.html
- Wenham (quoted by Coffman) and Constable: God freed Israel from Egypt to be his own servants, so it was wrong for an Israelite to be sold into slavery again. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/25-47.html
- Guzik: God's care for Israel rests on their being his servants first. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/leviticus/leviticus-25.cfm
- Clarke closes with Calmet: the Jubilee was meant to stop the rich keeping the poor in permanent slavery and buying up all the land. https://studylight.org/commentaries/acc/leviticus-25.html

## 2. Where interpreters differ
(Only Clarke, Calvin and Coffman are labelled by tradition on the pages.)

- **v. 35, who the "stranger" is.**
  - Matthew Henry says all people are brothers, so foreigners are included: https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/25-36.html
  - JFB also includes foreign residents: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/25-35.htm
  - The Pulpit Commentary prefers to limit it to Israelites, who are to be treated like resident foreigners: https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/leviticus-25.html
  - Barnes takes the same view: https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/25-35.html
  - Poole limits it to converts, since interest could be charged to other foreigners (Deut. 23:20): https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/25-35.htm
- **vv. 36–37, interest today.** JFB and Pulpit say the ban covers poor brothers, not modern business loans at legal rates. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/25-35.htm
  - Clarke (labelled Wesleyan/Methodist) defines usury as unlawful interest: https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/25-36.html
- **vv. 47–49, is the kinsman redeemer a picture of Christ?**
  - Yes, for Henry, Gill, the Pulpit Commentary and McGee. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lev/Lev_025.cfm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/25-49.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/leviticus-25.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/25-48.html
  - Maclaren still links it to Christ, but warns against calling the law "prophetic or typical": https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/25-48.htm
  - Precept Austin carries a long end-times reading of it: https://www.preceptaustin.org/kinsman-redeemer_-_the_goel
- **vv. 44–46, slavery.**
  - Barnes says Moses aimed to discourage and soften slavery, not end it straight away: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/25-44.htm
  - The Pulpit Commentary says the world "was not yet ready," as in Paul's day: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/25-44.htm
  - Constable says regulated slavery didn't violate basic human rights; abusing slaves did: https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/25-44.html
  - Maclaren says the law "regulated that accursed system": https://biblehub.com/study/leviticus/25-44.htm
  - Henry questions the use of Black people as slaves in English plantations: https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/25-44.html
  - Bible Hub's Q&A pages argue the law limits slavery and plants the seeds of abolition: https://biblehub.com/q/Why_does_Lev_25_44_allow_foreign_slaves.htm ; https://biblehub.com/q/Modern_view_on_Lev_25_44_rights.htm

## 3. Other views
- **Source criticism.** The Cambridge Bible assigns vv. 29–34 to the "P" source, and vv. 35–38 mainly to "H" with a little "P." It notes that Dillmann and Driver think "stranger or sojourner" in v. 35 may have been added later. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/25-35.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/25-29.htm
- **Christopher Wright (quoted by Constable).** Verses 39 onward are about a landholder pushed by poverty to mortgage his land and then sell himself. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/25-39.html
